item.title: Integrating computational fluid dynamics into introductory architectural education
item.description:
This study designed, implemented and evaluated a hybrid course integrating thermo-fluid-dynamics lectures with hands-on computational fluid dynamics (CFD) training for about 100 first-year architecture students in Japan. The course comprised 14 sessions: 10 lectures, three CFD training sessions and a review/feedback session. Students received feedback from the instructor and teaching assistants at an early checkpoint. Additional support included lecture-linked training materials, peer comparison and a whole-class review of common errors. The evaluation relied mainly on questionnaire responses about students’ self-rated understanding, interest and difficulties. Self-rated understanding increased after the CFD training, particularly for simulation set-up and interpretation. Over 90% of students reported greater interest in the built environment and a heightened awareness of thermal and airflow design. Reported difficulties shifted from software operation in the first practical session to boundary-condition-setting and visualisation in later sessions. The aligned lecture–training approach appears feasible at the introductory level and is associated with improved perceived understanding and engagement; as the findings rest on students’ perceptions, they are interpreted as changes in perceived learning rather than as causal effects.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

This course provides an example of how CFD can be taught to beginning architecture students. The findings suggest four points for course design: (1) aligning thermo-fluid-dynamics lectures with hands-on CFD on shared, simplified tasks makes abstract physical concepts visible and raises students’ perceived understanding and interest; (2) beginners’ difficulties shift from software operation to boundary conditions, modelling and result interpretation as tasks become open-ended, so support should be staged accordingly; (3) an early checkpoint with instructor and teaching-assistant feedback, lecture-linked training materials, peer comparison, and whole-class review of common errors together help students understand the lecture content and address these difficulties; and (4) early teaching of airflow and heat transfer may help students use CFD to assess airflow and thermal conditions in later design courses, with the long-term goal of supporting designs that reduce energy use and improve thermal comfort and indoor air quality.
